description: Between **1919** and **1933**, the **Bauhaus** school fused art, craft and industry in Germany. Closed by the Nazis, it still spread modern design across the world.

hero.hook: A German school that lasted 14 years designed the modern world, from the chair to the smartphone.

blocks.text: The **Bauhaus** (1919-1933) was the most influential art and design school of the 20th century. Founded in Germany just after the First World War, it rejected the useless decoration of the 19th century. Its goal: to invent a simple language, fit for the industrial age.
By fusing art, craft and technique, it laid the foundations of modern [[Functionalism in design]]. Its life was short. Its legacy is everywhere.

In **1919**, the architect **Walter Gropius** founded the Bauhaus in **Weimar**. His manifesto was blunt: the final goal of all creation is architecture. No more border between noble “fine arts” and second-class “applied arts.” Craft became the base of everything.

blocks.caption: The Bauhaus: a school where you learn by making

blocks.text: Every workshop had two masters: an artist and a craftsman. Figures such as [[Wassily Kandinsky]], the Russian abstract painter, taught there. The school also talked with [[De Stijl]], the Dutch movement obsessed with the rectangle and with pure colors.

sections.title: Weimar 1919: abolishing the hierarchy of the arts

blocks.text: Once it moved to **Dessau**, the school turned toward mass production. Its famous slogan: **“form follows function”**. Ornament was judged useless. The aim was objects that were simple, beautiful and easy to make in a factory.
**Marcel Breuer**, a teacher at the Bauhaus, reused the tubular steel of bicycles to invent light chairs. A factory material became living room furniture.
The workshops tested metal, glass, textiles and typography. The goal was no longer the one-off luxury piece. It was the standard object, within reach of as many people as possible.

The school made people uneasy. It was accused of being too modern, too international, too far to the left. After a last spell in Berlin under **Mies van der Rohe** came the [[Shutdown by the Nazis (1933)]]. The regime saw it as “cultural Bolshevism.”

blocks.caption: Mies van der Rohe: the last head of the Bauhaus, then exile in America

blocks.text: The shutdown turned into a broadcast. The masters left for the United States, Britain and Palestine. In Tel Aviv, their ideas fed the [[White City of Tel Aviv]], a vast district of white modern architecture.

sections.title: Closed by the Nazis, saved by exile

blocks.text: Today the Bauhaus legacy is everywhere: flat-pack furniture, plain buildings, clean interfaces, [[sans-serif]] type with no little strokes at the ends of the letters. IKEA, airports, our phones: the geometric clarity of the Bauhaus has become the ordinary scenery of the world.

events.title: Founded in Weimar

events.detail: Exile spreads the Bauhaus around the world.
events.title: Nazi shutdown

blocks.text: In just 14 years, the Bauhaus invented the modern idea of design: less ornament, more function, objects that are beautiful because they are useful. Closing it for political reasons only sped up its conquest of everyday life.

sections.title: A design so obvious it turned invisible
